title: How To Make Dhaniya Panjiri: A Traditional Janmashtami Recipe
excerpt: This fragrant, no-grain sweet made from roasted coriander seeds, ghee, and dry fruits is the essential bhog offering for Lord Krishna's birthday.
body:
• Dhaniya panjiri is a traditional no-grain sweet made from roasted coriander seeds, ghee, nuts, and powdered sugar — a staple bhog offering during Janmashtami celebrations.
  • The recipe requires just 30 minutes and uses pantry-friendly ingredients including coriander seeds, makhana, almonds, cashews, dried coconut, and cardamom.
  • Coriander-based panjiri is light and sattvic, making it ideal for breaking the Janmashtami fast that devotees observe until midnight.
  • The dish is traditionally offered to Laddu Gopal along with butter and curd during the Nishita Puja window, which fell between 11:57 PM on September 4 and 12:43 AM on September 5 this year.

Janmashtami, the festival celebrating Lord Krishna's birth, brings with it one of the most beloved prasad traditions in Indian households: dhaniya panjiri. This fragrant, crumbly sweet made from roasted coriander seeds is considered an essential part of the 56-item chappan bhog offered to Laddu Gopal, and devotees across North India prepare it fresh for the midnight worship that marks Krishna's arrival.

Unlike wheat-based sweets, dhaniya panjiri uses no grains at all, making it perfectly aligned with the strict fasting rules many devotees follow through the day. Coriander seeds are considered sattvic — pure and light — which is why they hold a central place in Janmashtami prasad traditions. The dish is also naturally gluten-free.

Ingredients You Will Need

This recipe yields enough panjiri for a small family's bhog offering and prasad distribution. Preparation takes roughly 30 minutes.

  • 1 cup whole coriander seeds (sabut dhaniya)
  • 2–3 tablespoons desi ghee
  • ½ cup makhana (fox nuts), roughly chopped
  • ¼ cup almonds, chopped
  • ¼ cup cashews, chopped
  • 2 tablespoons melon seeds
  • ¼ cup grated dried coconut
  • ½ cup powdered sugar or bura
  • ½ teaspoon green cardamom powder
  • 2 tablespoons raisins (optional)
  • 4–5 fresh tulsi leaves for garnish

"Place whole coriander seeds in a clean, dry pan over low flame."

Step-by-Step Recipe

  1. Dry-roast the coriander seeds. Place whole coriander seeds in a clean, dry pan over low flame. Roast for 2–3 minutes, stirring constantly, until they become fragrant. Do not let them brown or burn. Transfer to a plate and allow them to cool completely.
  2. Grind to a coarse powder. Once cooled, grind the roasted coriander seeds in a dry grinder to a fine or coarse powder, depending on your preference. Set aside.
  3. Roast the makhana and dry fruits. In the same pan, heat 1 tablespoon of ghee. Add makhana, almonds, cashews, and melon seeds. Sauté on medium flame for 2–3 minutes until the makhana turns crispy and the nuts are lightly golden. Transfer to a large mixing bowl.
  4. Toast the dried coconut. Add grated dried coconut to the pan and roast on low flame for 2–3 minutes until aromatic. Add to the mixing bowl with the nuts.
  5. Cook the coriander powder in ghee. Add the remaining ghee to the pan. Tip in the ground coriander powder and sauté on low flame for 1–2 minutes, stirring continuously. The powder will release a deep, warm aroma. Transfer to the mixing bowl.
  6. Combine with sugar and cardamom. Allow all roasted ingredients to cool down fully — this is important, as adding sugar to hot ingredients can cause it to melt and turn sticky. Once cool, add powdered sugar, cardamom powder, and raisins if using. Mix everything gently until well combined.
  7. Serve as bhog. Transfer the panjiri to a clean silver or brass bowl. Garnish with tulsi leaves. Offer to Laddu Gopal alongside butter and fresh curd at midnight.

Tips for the Best Panjiri

Nutritionist Karishmma Chawla and veteran home cooks recommend a few key pointers: never add sugar to hot coriander powder, as it will clump; use clean, dedicated utensils for preparing prasad; and avoid over-roasting any ingredient, which can introduce bitterness. If you prefer a richer version, pumpkin seeds and chironji can be added alongside the almonds and cashews.

The panjiri stores well in an airtight container for up to a week at room temperature, making it practical for distribution among family and neighbors during the festival.

Why Coriander Holds Special Significance

Dhaniya panjiri's association with Janmashtami runs deep in Hindu tradition. Coriander is believed to be among Lord Krishna's favorite offerings, and its cooling properties make it well-suited for consumption after a full day of fasting. The dry, crumbly texture of panjiri also travels well, which is why it remains the prasad of choice for community distribution at temples and neighborhood celebrations.

With Janmashtami 2026 observed on September 4–5 and Nandotsav and Dahi Handi celebrations continuing on September 5, households across the diaspora are preparing their bhog platters. Whether you follow a family recipe passed down through generations or are making dhaniya panjiri for the first time, the process is forgiving and the result is always worth sharing.
